skills.title: Add configurable file-output line-ending normalization
skills.summary: Expose a constrained line-ending policy with a backward-compatible platform default, propagate the selected mode from application configuration into the shared I/O service, translate it to the text-runtime newline value, and enforce it at the centralized file-write boundary so all existing writers inherit LF, CRLF, or platform behavior.

ordered_actions.action: Define user-selectable platform, LF, and CRLF modes while retaining platform translation as the default.
Pass the parsed mode from application startup into the shared InputOutput service.
Map the semantic mode to the text I/O newline argument: null for platform behavior, "\n" for LF, or "\r\n" for CRLF.
Supply the mapped value to open() in the centralized write_text method, allowing editing and ancillary write paths to inherit the policy without individual changes.

preconditions: Application output is routed through a shared text-writing service.
The runtime text API supports explicit newline translation control.
The configuration layer can constrain the accepted line-ending modes.
exclusions: Does not preserve each input file's preexisting line-ending convention automatically.
Does not cover file writes that bypass the shared write_text boundary.
Does not establish byte-level correctness through tests; the pinned change added no dedicated tests.
failure_modes: A write path that bypasses the shared I/O service will not inherit the configured policy.
Incorrect semantic-to-runtime mapping can emit unintended line endings.
Failing to propagate the parsed option into the shared service leaves output at the compatibility default.

payload.goal: Make line endings for generated and updated text files explicitly configurable across existing output call sites.
payload.test_evidence: No dedicated tests were added or found for the option.

skills.title: Make exact text edits independent of line-ending encoding
skills.summary: Detect the source file's newline style, canonicalize the file content and edit operands to LF, perform existence checks, normalized uniqueness enforcement, no-op detection, replacement, and semantic diff generation on that canonical representation, then restore the detected CRLF or LF style before writing. This allows LF-only edit input to modify equivalent CRLF content without changing the file's established line-ending style.
preconditions: The operation edits a text file by locating an exact old-text region and replacing it with new text.
CRLF and LF differences should be treated as encoding differences rather than semantic differences.
The source file's detected line-ending style should be retained when the edited content is persisted.

case_actions.action: Detect and retain the source file's line-ending style before canonicalization.
Normalize file content, old text, and replacement text to LF before exact matching and replacement.
Run existence, occurrence-count, uniqueness, index, and no-op checks against the canonical text so equivalent CRLF and LF regions are handled consistently.
Apply the replacement to the canonical file content.
Generate the user-facing diff from canonical pre-edit and post-edit content to avoid newline-only noise.
Convert the completed canonical content back to the detected source style immediately before writing.

failure_modes: Matching raw file content against differently encoded edit text can falsely report that the target text is absent.
Counting occurrences before normalization can allow logically duplicated targets with different newline encodings to bypass the single-match constraint.
Writing canonical LF content directly can unintentionally change a CRLF file's line-ending style.
Generating diffs from raw encodings can obscure or inflate the semantic edit with newline-format differences.

response.rationale: Both workflows address line endings at text-write boundaries, but they solve different problems and are not semantically interchangeable. The candidate canonicalizes file and edit text for exact matching, uniqueness checks, replacement, and semantic diffing, then restores each source file's detected line-ending style. The peer exposes a configurable application-wide output policy and applies LF, CRLF, or platform translation through shared I/O; it explicitly does not preserve each file's existing convention automatically and does not address normalized matching, duplicate detection, or diff generation. Neither subsumes the other, and merging them would conflate preservation-based editing with policy-driven output normalization.

skills.title: Decode a native NUL-terminated UTF-16 string through a pointer-width variable
skills.summary: When an FFI returns a raw address for a NUL-terminated UTF-16 string, serialize that address into a buffer sized to `sizeof(void *)` and pass the pointer variable to the FFI library's native UTF-16 string decoder. This avoids arbitrary external-memory bounds and error-prone manual terminator scanning.
skills.applicability: FFI bindings where a native API returns a numeric address to a NUL-terminated string and the FFI decoder expects a pointer variable rather than the pointee bytes.

skills.title: Preserve the original native address for allocator-matched release
skills.summary: Keep the raw address returned by a native API separate from the decoded managed string, and pass that unchanged address to the allocator-mandated deallocation function after decoding. Decoding must not replace, truncate, or otherwise alter the ownership token used for release.
skills.applicability: Native out-parameters whose returned allocation must be released by a specific platform or library deallocator.

skills.title: Verify pointer marshalling at both 32-bit and 64-bit widths
skills.summary: Test pointer serialization with nontrivial numeric addresses at four-byte and eight-byte pointer widths, asserting the exact width and bytes supplied to the decoder as well as preservation of the original address passed to native cleanup.
skills.applicability: FFI code that converts numeric addresses into pointer buffers and must behave correctly on both 32-bit and 64-bit processes.

skills.title: Test native string decoding with live FFI-compatible buffers
skills.summary: Exercise the real FFI string decoder over test-owned native-compatible buffers whose lifetime spans the synchronous dereference. Include UTF-16 cases that expose byte-scanning errors, surrogate pairs, NUL termination, and strings beyond any removed fixed-size boundary, while also verifying cleanup.
skills.applicability: FFI string-decoding changes where mocks alone cannot validate actual pointer dereference, encoding behavior, terminator handling, buffer lifetime, or removal of an artificial size limit.

skills.title: Replace bounded native UTF-16 views with pointer-width FFI decoding while preserving ownership
skills.summary: For an FFI out-parameter that returns an allocator-owned, NUL-terminated UTF-16 address, trace the decoding and cleanup path, remove the arbitrary external-memory view and manual terminator scan, marshal the address through a variable sized to the process pointer width, decode it with the FFI library's native UTF-16 decoder, and retain the unchanged raw address for allocator-matched release. Validate the complete production path with 32-bit and 64-bit pointer marshalling plus live-buffer cases covering UTF-16 byte patterns, surrogate pairs, NUL termination, and strings beyond the removed fixed bound.

case_workflow.goal: Eliminate unsafe or truncating fixed-size reads of allocator-owned native UTF-16 strings without breaking native ownership and cleanup semantics.

actions.operation: Trace the native out-parameter from allocation through decoding, caller consumption, and allocator-mandated release.
Replace the fixed-size external view and manual UTF-16 terminator scan with the FFI library's native NUL-terminated UTF-16 decoding.
Serialize the numeric native address into a pointer variable restricted to sizeof(void *) before passing it to the decoder.
Keep the original returned address separate from the managed decoded string and pass it unchanged to the required deallocator.
Verify exact pointer bytes and widths for both four-byte and eight-byte pointer environments, including the address supplied to cleanup.

Exercise the real decoder over live test-owned buffers containing adversarial UTF-16 data, explicit NUL termination, surrogate pairs, and content longer than the removed fixed bound, while checking deallocation and COM cleanup.

preconditions: The native API returns a raw address to a NUL-terminated UTF-16 allocation.
The FFI decoder expects a pointer variable rather than the numeric address directly.
The process pointer width is available from the FFI runtime.
The original allocation must be released by a specific native deallocator after synchronous decoding.
failure_modes: Passing a buffer with the wrong pointer width can truncate or corrupt the native address.
Scanning UTF-16 byte-by-byte can mistake a zero byte inside a code unit for termination.
Using an arbitrary external-view length can truncate valid data or read beyond the actual allocation.
Replacing or truncating the raw address during decoding can cause an invalid or mismatched native free.
Allowing a test-owned native-compatible buffer to expire before synchronous decoding can invalidate the dereference.

skills.title: Audit and route all runtime state through the configured application home
skills.summary: Audit runtime storage paths for direct operating-system-home or literal ~/.hermes construction; replace each bypass in module-level constants and operational call sites with the canonical home resolver, an already-resolved application-home value, or equivalent environment-aware logic while preserving the legacy fallback; then configure an isolated HERMES_HOME in focused tests and verify both discovery reads and generated-file writes are rooted beneath it.
preconditions: The application defines a configurable runtime-home setting with a legacy default fallback.
Some runtime state paths bypass that setting by deriving directly from the operating-system home directory or a literal default path.

case_actions.action: Identify storage constants and runtime call sites that construct the legacy home path directly instead of using the configured application home.
Route module-level storage roots and operational paths through the shared resolver, an existing resolved home value, or equivalent environment-aware fallback logic.
Preserve the existing ~/.hermes fallback when HERMES_HOME is not configured.
Update focused tests to set HERMES_HOME to a temporary directory and assert observable read and write behavior beneath that root.
Search for and complete remaining bypasses after the initial conversion, including residual debug-log and test paths.

failure_modes: Converting only prominent call sites leaves residual state under the operating-system home and breaks instance isolation.
Updating operational code but not import-time constants can retain paths resolved from the wrong root.
Changing the custom-root behavior without preserving the default fallback can regress existing installations.
Tests that patch Path.home() rather than HERMES_HOME do not verify the configured-home contract.
Testing only one path category can miss unconverted readers or writers elsewhere in the repository.
exclusions: This workflow does not establish dedicated behavioral coverage for every converted path; the episode directly updates tests only for channel-session discovery and clipboard image storage.
This workflow does not claim that the full test suite or CI was executed successfully because such evidence was unavailable.

skills.title: Harden ordered registry overrides against stale duplicate entries
skills.summary: Trace configuration inputs through registry mutation and first-match consumer lookup to confirm that earlier duplicate keys can shadow a later override. For each incoming setting, mutate the shared registry in place to remove every entry with the same key, then append the replacement as the sole authoritative entry while preserving list identity for existing references. Confirm the resulting ordering and uniqueness semantics; add duplicate-key regression coverage when possible, noting that this episode supplied no such automated test.

steps.action: Follow ordered settings-file loading into the registry and inspect the consumer's first-exact-match behavior to establish how stale earlier entries shadow appended overrides.
Filter out every registry entry whose name equals the incoming setting name rather than removing only the first match.
Apply the filtering through slice assignment so aliases to the shared registry continue to observe the authoritative contents.
Append the incoming setting after filtering, leaving exactly one entry for its name and ensuring first-match lookup selects the replacement.
Check duplicate-name behavior and shared-list identity; introduce a regression test with multiple pre-existing same-name entries when test changes are in scope.

preconditions: Configuration settings are stored in an ordered mutable registry.
Overrides are keyed by model name or an equivalent stable key.
Consumers can select the first matching registry entry.
Other code may retain references to the registry list.
failure_modes: Removing only one same-key entry leaves another stale entry able to win first-match lookup.
Rebinding the registry variable disconnects existing aliases from subsequent updates.
Appending before removing duplicates can preserve or create incorrect precedence.
Testing only a single pre-existing match does not cover the duplicate-shadowing failure.
exclusions: This workflow does not define precedence for consumers that intentionally use last-match lookup or merge all matching entries.
Automated duplicate-name regression validation was not present in the episode.

skills.title: Normalize heterogeneous provider HTTP errors
skills.summary: Convert an unknown thrown value into a common representation containing its message, HTTP status, response body, and whether the message already carries that body. Probe known SDK shapes such as statusCode, status, $metadata.httpStatusCode, $response.statusCode, body, error, and $response.body, while safely serializing non-Error throws and ignoring empty parsed bodies.

skills.title: Bound surfaced provider error bodies
skills.summary: Trim an extracted response body and cap its user-visible length at 4000 characters with an explicit truncation suffix, preventing oversized gateway responses from overwhelming displayed errors.

skills.title: Format provider errors without duplicating response bodies
skills.summary: Render a normalized error using its HTTP status and response body when the SDK message is opaque, optionally preserving a provider-specific prefix. Keep the original message when no useful status/body exists or when that message already includes the extracted body.

skills.title: Append supplemental raw error metadata only when absent
skills.summary: Before adding supplemental raw provider metadata to a formatted error, check whether the same text is already present so the diagnostic appears exactly once.

skills.title: Regression-test provider error-body passthrough
skills.summary: Inject synthetic SDK-shaped failures through provider catch paths and assert that user-visible output includes available status and response reasons while preserving required prefixes or hints and suppressing duplicate body or metadata text.

skills.title: Surface hidden HTTP error details across provider SDK paths
skills.summary: Replace message-only provider error handling with a shared workflow that normalizes heterogeneous thrown values, extracts and bounds available HTTP status and response-body details, formats useful diagnostics without duplicating body text, preserves provider-specific prefixes and Bedrock guidance, conditionally appends supplemental OpenRouter metadata, integrates the result into all affected provider catch paths, and regression-tests representative SDK error shapes and user-visible outputs.

ordered_actions.action: Convert each caught provider value into a common message, HTTP status, response body, and body-presence representation by probing supported SDK field shapes and safely serializing non-Error throws.
Discard empty extracted bodies and trim and cap useful bodies at 4000 characters before surfacing them.

Use status and body when the original SDK message is opaque, retain the original message when it already contains the body or no better details exist, and preserve required provider prefixes and Bedrock's retention hint.

Route the normalized formatting through Azure OpenAI Responses, Bedrock Converse, Google Generative AI, Google Vertex, OpenAI Codex Responses, OpenAI Completions, OpenAI Responses, and OpenRouter Images catch paths.
For OpenAI Completions using OpenRouter metadata, append metadata.raw only when the formatted diagnostic does not already contain the same text.

Exercise helper and provider catch paths with synthetic Mistral-, OpenAI-, Google-, and Bedrock-shaped failures and verify status/body passthrough, truncation, message and prefix preservation, Bedrock guidance retention, and duplicate suppression.

preconditions: Provider SDK failures may retain useful HTTP status or response-body data outside Error.message.
Affected catch paths produce user-visible provider error messages and can call shared normalization and formatting utilities.

skills.title: Propagate entity provenance into an editor
skills.summary: Carry a directory entry’s stable provenance or ownership marker through the editor target and component props, then use it to expose route-owned controls only for user-declared entities rather than adapter-provided entries.
skills.applicability: Use when editability depends on how an entity was introduced and that classification currently exists only in the listing or directory layer.
skills.failure_cause: The editor lacked the directory entry’s declared status, so it could not safely distinguish editable user-declared routes from adapter-shipped routes.

skills.title: Edit an identity override while preserving layered fallback semantics
skills.summary: Persist a nonblank display-name override with a minimal path set operation, but translate clearing or whitespace-only input into an unset operation so lower configuration layers or the stable entity id can provide the effective name.
skills.applicability: Use for optional configuration overrides whose removal must reveal inherited or default values rather than store an empty value.
skills.failure_cause: The existing editor did not expose the route-owned display-name field, and naïvely storing an empty string would suppress the intended configuration fallback.

skills.title: Populate an editor select from the owning schema
skills.summary: Reuse the same schema-derived protocol choices in creation and editing flows, and represent an absent effective value with an explicit localized unselected option so legacy or handwritten configurations remain editable without inventing a protocol.
skills.applicability: Use when a configurable enum is defined by an adapter or namespace schema and existing records may omit the field.
skills.failure_cause: The edit flow lacked the protocol control and could otherwise drift from creation-time choices or misrepresent configurations with no stored protocol.

skills.title: Refresh identity-dependent feedback after a rename
skills.summary: After applying an edit, reload the authoritative directory and resolve the entity by stable id before constructing confirmation text, ensuring the notice uses the newly computed display name rather than the name captured when editing began.
skills.applicability: Use when a mutation can change a displayed identity and post-save feedback depends on refreshed or composed state.
skills.failure_cause: Save confirmation retained the editor’s opening display name, causing successful renames to be announced under the stale name.

skills.title: Guard shared select presentation
skills.summary: Apply the common select styling class to all related dropdowns and add a static test that rejects unstyled select elements, preventing individual controls from regressing to inconsistent native-arrow presentation.
skills.applicability: Use when native controls require a shared visual treatment across multiple creation and editing surfaces.
skills.failure_cause: Protocol dropdowns could omit the shared select class and render inconsistent operating-system-native arrows.

skills.title: Add edit parity for fields owned by a declared provider route
skills.summary: Extend an existing provider editor to support fields previously available only during creation: propagate the directory entry’s declared provenance into the editor, gate route-owned controls to declared pi-ai providers, populate protocol choices from the owning schema with an explicit unselected state, persist display-name and protocol changes through minimal path operations while treating a cleared name as an unset for layered fallback, then reload the authoritative directory and resolve the provider by stable id before publishing rename-sensitive confirmation. Verify visibility, mutation and fallback semantics, persisted browser behavior, accessibility structure, and shared select presentation.
preconditions: The directory exposes a stable provider id and a declared provenance marker.
The editor already supports minimal path-based set and unset mutations.
The owning adapter namespace schema exposes the supported protocol choices.
The provider directory can be reloaded after a successful mutation.

payload.goal: Make creation-time identity and protocol fields editable when reopening a user-declared provider without exposing route-owned controls on adapter-provided entries or breaking layered configuration semantics.

ordered_actions.action: Carry the directory entry’s declared marker through the editor target and component props so the editor can distinguish user-declared routes from adapter-provided entries.

For declared pi-ai routes, expose the route-level display-name and API-protocol controls, reuse schema-derived protocol choices, and preserve a localized unselected state when no protocol is configured.

Persist nonblank identity overrides and protocol changes through the existing minimal path-operation flow, translating a cleared or whitespace-only display name into an unset so lower layers or the stable route id provide the effective name.
After applying the mutation, reload the authoritative provider directory and resolve the edited provider by stable id before constructing confirmation text, preventing stale pre-rename feedback.
Apply and statically enforce the shared select styling across the creation and editing protocol controls.
Validate the complete flow with component mutation and fallback tests, a browser test that reopens and persists both fields, and an accessibility snapshot of the expanded editor.

failure_modes: If provenance is not propagated, route-owned controls cannot be gated correctly and may remain unavailable or appear for adapter-provided entries.
If clearing the display name is stored as an empty override instead of an unset, lower configuration layers and id-based fallback are masked.
If protocol options are duplicated rather than schema-derived, creation and editing can offer inconsistent or unsupported values.
If a missing protocol is coerced to a concrete value, legacy or handwritten configurations are silently changed.
If confirmation is built from the editor’s captured identity before reloading, a successful rename can announce the old display name.

skills.title: Detect unmerged paths after applying a Git stash
skills.summary: After `git stash apply`, query `git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U` and treat any reported unmerged path as restoration failure, even when the apply command returned zero.

skills.title: Reset a conflicted stash restoration to HEAD
skills.summary: When stash application fails or leaves unmerged paths, run `git reset --hard HEAD` to remove partially applied tracked-file changes and conflict markers while retaining the stash as the recovery copy.

skills.title: Report retained-stash recovery after cleanup failure
skills.summary: After resetting a failed restoration, exit nonzero and tell the user that the working tree was reset, the saved changes remain in the stash, and which `git stash apply` command can be used for manual recovery.

skills.title: Test stash conflicts hidden by a successful exit status
skills.summary: Regression-test a stash apply that returns zero while Git still reports an unmerged path, asserting that the conflict cleanup, nonzero exit, and retained-stash recovery guidance are triggered.

skills.title: Recover an update safely when autostash restoration conflicts
skills.summary: During an update, preserve local edits in an autostash, pull the new revision, and attempt restoration from the existing finally path. After applying the stash, inspect Git for unmerged paths rather than trusting the apply exit status alone. If application fails or conflicts remain, hard-reset tracked files to the updated HEAD, retain the stash as the recovery copy, report the cleanup and exact manual recovery command, and exit with status 1; otherwise continue the existing stash lookup and drop flow.
preconditions: An update operation has saved local changes in an identifiable Git stash before pulling updates.
Stash restoration is invoked after the pull attempt, including from the update operation's finally path.
case_actions: Apply the saved stash after the update attempt.
Treat either a nonzero stash-apply status or any unmerged path as restoration failure.
On restoration failure, run `git reset --hard HEAD` to return tracked files to the updated revision.
Retain the stash, report that the working tree was reset, provide the manual `git stash apply` recovery command, and exit with status 1.
When restoration succeeds without unmerged paths, continue the existing stash lookup and drop flow.
failure_modes: A stash apply may return nonzero after partially modifying tracked files.
A stash apply may return zero while Git still reports unmerged paths.
exclusions: Does not drop the stash after a failed or conflicted restoration.
Does not rely solely on the stash-apply process exit status to determine restoration success.
Does not claim cleanup of untracked files, because `git reset --hard HEAD` addresses tracked working-tree and index state.

tests: Explicit stash-apply failure triggers one hard reset, a nonzero exit, and clean-state messaging.
Zero-status stash application with a reported unmerged path triggers the same reset and retained-stash recovery path.
validation.execution_status: Test behavior is supported by committed test code; the focused tests were not locally executed because pytest was unavailable.

skills.title: Convert an absent service response into an explicit domain failure
skills.summary: Immediately validate a nullable response from an external or model-backed helper and raise a descriptive domain-level exception before using the value in string or message construction. This replaces an incidental downstream type error with a failure that identifies the operation and relevant service or model.
skills.applicability: Use when a helper may return `None` on failure but its caller requires a concrete value.
limitations: The episode provides no regression test for this behavior.
This operation classifies the immediate failure but does not define recovery or state preservation.

skills.title: Report an expected background-task failure through the application error channel
skills.summary: Catch the explicit exception expected from a background operation at the worker boundary and forward its message through the application's user-facing error-reporting channel, preventing the failure from appearing only as an unhandled worker-thread exception.
skills.applicability: Use when an asynchronous worker can receive a known, intentionally classified failure and the application has a standard mechanism for surfacing errors to users.
limitations: The caught path does not assign a safe replacement result; subsequent code may still consume `None` and fail.
Catching a broad exception class such as `ValueError` is appropriate only when that class is part of the worker's expected failure contract.

skills.title: Surface a failed chat-history summarization at the background-worker boundary
skills.summary: When chat-history summarization returns no response, convert the absent result into a descriptive model-specific exception before constructing summary content, then catch that expected exception at the background worker boundary and report it through the application's user-facing error channel instead of allowing an incidental type error to escape from the worker thread. This workflow improves failure classification and visibility but does not provide recovery: the failed path can still leave the summarized-history result unset and cause a later message-assembly failure.
preconditions: The summarization transport or model helper may return None rather than a usable summary.
Summarization executes inside a background worker with access to the application's user-facing error-reporting channel.
failure_modes: Catching and reporting the exception without preserving or replacing the original history can leave summarized_done_messages as None.
The join path may assign the unset summarized result to done_messages, causing later outgoing-message assembly to fail.
The behavior and emitted error message are not covered by a regression test in this episode.
exclusions: Does not establish successful recovery from summarization failure.
Does not preserve the original chat history after the reported failure.
Does not validate downstream state before replacing done_messages.

skills.title: Guard request admission during an exclusive lifecycle operation
skills.summary: At the shared request entry point, check the existing active-operation marker and reject ordinary side-effecting requests before interception, transformation, message construction, persistence, or execution. skills.title: Propagate preflight rejection through an asynchronous request contract
skills.summary: Report an admission exception as preflight failure and rethrow it so an asynchronous caller emits an error rather than acknowledging a request that never reached execution. This applies when caller success is conditional on a preflight callback and failure is obtained from the rejected request promise.

skills.title: Deterministically test a lifecycle-request race
skills.summary: Pause the lifecycle operation at a controlled hook, submit the conflicting request while the active-state marker is set, assert rejection and the absence of execution, in-memory, and persistence side effects, and release the paused operation in cleanup to prevent a hanging test.

skills.title: Prevent concurrent prompt mutation during manual compaction
skills.summary: Use the manual-compaction controller as the exclusive-operation marker, reject ordinary prompts at the shared session entry point before interception, message construction, persistence, or agent execution, preserve extension-command dispatch by placing the guard after that exemption, propagate the thrown admission error through the existing preflight contract so RPC callers receive failure rather than success, and verify the behavior by pausing compaction deterministically and asserting rejection with no execution, in-memory, or persisted side effects.
preconditions: The exclusive lifecycle operation exposes a reliable marker that remains active for its full mutation interval and is cleared during cleanup.
Conflicting requests share an admission boundary where they can be rejected before side effects begin.
The asynchronous caller treats preflight failure plus promise rejection as request failure rather than acknowledgment.

case_actions.action: At the shared prompt boundary, inspect the active manual-compaction marker after exempt extension-command dispatch and reject ordinary prompts before input handling or message construction.
Allow the admission exception to trigger preflightResult(false) and be rethrown so asynchronous RPC handling emits an error and never reports successful acceptance.

Pause compaction at a controlled hook, submit conflicting direct and RPC prompts while the marker is active, assert rejection and absence of agent, history, and persistence effects, and release compaction in cleanup.

failure_modes: Placing the guard after interception or message construction permits partial side effects before rejection.
Placing the guard before explicitly exempt command dispatch unnecessarily disables commands intended to remain available during compaction.
Reporting preflight success before the guard causes RPC clients to receive an acknowledgment for a prompt that cannot execute.
Using timing delays instead of a controlled pause makes the concurrency regression test nondeterministic.
Failing to release the paused compaction operation during test cleanup can hang the test suite.

skills.title: Project a durable terminal event into a typed conversation node
skills.summary: Match a specific durable turn-ending reason and materialize a typed conversation node from the terminal event itself, allowing the state to be reconstructed during live updates, window rebuilds, and history replay without depending on the corresponding start event.
skills.applicability: Use when an event-sourced conversation log already records a meaningful terminal condition but the conversation model does not expose that condition as a durable UI node.
skills.operation: Filter terminal events by exact reason, derive the owning turn and last-step metadata from available durable state, and emit a discriminated conversation node while excluding unrelated completion and error reasons.
constraints: Match the exact terminal reason rather than treating every turn end identically.
Derivation must work when the loaded event window omits the owning turn-start event.
Completed and error turns must remain semantically distinct.

skills.title: Anchor a terminal notice before the turn tail
skills.summary: Assign a synthetic terminal notice an ordering anchor after the final assistant output but before the finalized turn tail, keeping the notice contextually adjacent to the truncated output while preserving tail-owned actions.
skills.applicability: Use when adding a synthetic status node to an ordered conversation and the existing final tail node must remain last because it owns branch, retry, or other terminal actions.
skills.operation: Compute the notice sequence from the closing assistant or terminal-event position using a dedicated synthetic offset that sorts before the turn-tail offset.
constraints: The notice must follow retained assistant output.
The turn tail must remain the final node.
Ordering must be stable during both live assembly and replay.

skills.title: Render localized guidance for truncated output
skills.summary: Render output-cap termination as a warning status with locale-owned explanatory and recovery text, making clear that the reply was cut off, existing output remains valid, and the user can request continuation without presenting the condition as an error.
skills.applicability: Use when partial output is retained after a non-error terminal condition and users need both an explanation and a concrete recovery action.
skills.operation: Map the dedicated terminal node kind to a warning-styled renderer whose title and guidance come from localization resources and whose presentation is distinct from terminal errors.
constraints: Do not discard or obscure the partial assistant output.
Do not reuse failure wording or error styling for a non-error truncation state.
User-facing text must be owned by locale resources rather than embedded in projection logic.

skills.title: Surface a durable terminal state throughout the conversation UI
skills.summary: Carry a previously unrepresented durable turn-ending condition through the public node model, event-derived conversation projection, stable turn-relative ordering, renderer registration, localization, replay paths, and assembled UI verification so users see retained partial output and actionable recovery guidance without confusing the condition with completion or failure.
preconditions: The durable session log already records a distinct terminal event reason that can be matched without relying on an earlier start event.
The conversation pipeline supports typed projected nodes, deterministic synthetic ordering, keyed renderers, and locale-owned text.
The terminal condition must remain semantically distinct from normal completion and terminal error.
skills.case_workflow_goal: Make max-token termination visible as a persistent, localized truncation notice during live display, window rebuild, and history replay while retaining partial assistant output and turn-tail actions.

case_actions.action: Extend the public conversation-node model with a typed node for the durable terminal condition.
Register an event-derived definition that matches only max-token turn-end events and reconstructs the node directly from terminal-event data, including turn, sequence, timestamp, and last-step state.

Assign the notice a deterministic synthetic anchor after the closing assistant output and before the finalized turn tail so the explanation stays adjacent to truncated content while tail-owned branch actions remain available.
Wire the new node kind into conversation definition registration, renderer dispatch, and finalized snapshot contribution handling.
Render the condition as a warning rather than an error, using locale-owned English and Chinese text that explains truncation, confirms earlier output remains, and suggests requesting continuation.
Add durable fixture history containing partial assistant output followed by the terminal reason, enabling assembled reconstruction without a live provider.

Verify positive matching, exclusion of completed and error turns, ordering relative to assistant output and turn tail, replay from a window lacking turn-start, localized presentation, warning semantics, and retention of partial output.

exclusions: Do not derive the notice from transient UI state or require the corresponding turn-start event, because either approach can lose the notice during partial-window rebuild or history replay.
Do not classify max-token termination as a normal completion or reuse the terminal-error presentation.
Do not place the notice after the turn tail when doing so would displace or interfere with tail-owned actions.
Do not discard or replace partial assistant output when adding the terminal notice.

skills.title: Resolve a configurable compression floor safely
skills.summary: Convert an optional context-floor override into an effective token floor: use 64,000 when absent and clamp explicit values to the hard safety minimum of 16,000.

skills.title: Parse and propagate compression-floor configuration
skills.summary: Read compression.minimum_context_floor during agent initialization, coerce valid values to integers, treat malformed values as no override, and pass the result into ContextCompressor.

skills.title: Apply the effective floor to compression thresholds
skills.summary: Store the resolved minimum context floor in ContextCompressor and use it when calculating compression thresholds both at construction time and after model updates.

skills.title: Validate auxiliary models against the effective floor
skills.summary: Determine auxiliary compression-model feasibility using the compressor's configured effective floor instead of a fixed 64,000-token requirement, allowing smaller models when the floor is deliberately lowered.

skills.title: Invalidate cached agents when the compression floor changes
skills.summary: Include compression.minimum_context_floor in the gateway's agent-construction cache signature so changing the setting causes the cached agent to be rebuilt.

skills.title: Configure and consistently enforce a lower safe compression floor
skills.summary: Accept an optional compression minimum-context floor, normalize it to a 64,000-token default with a 16,000-token hard safety minimum, propagate the effective value through compressor construction and model-update threshold calculations, validate auxiliary compression models against that same value, and invalidate cached gateway agents whenever the configuration changes.

ordered_actions.action: Read compression.minimum_context_floor during agent initialization, coerce valid values to integers, treat malformed or absent values as no override, and forward the result to ContextCompressor.
Resolve the supplied override into an effective floor by retaining the 64,000-token default when absent and clamping explicit values to at least 16,000 tokens.
Store the effective floor in ContextCompressor and apply it when calculating thresholds during both initial construction and later model updates.
Use the compressor's effective floor, rather than a fixed 64,000-token requirement, when deciding whether an auxiliary compression model has sufficient context capacity.
Include compression.minimum_context_floor in the gateway cache signature so configuration changes reconstruct the agent with the new floor.

preconditions: Agent compression thresholds are derived from model context capacity.
Agent construction may be cached by the gateway.
Any auxiliary compression model must have a context window at least as large as the effective compression floor.
postconditions: Absent or malformed configuration preserves the 64,000-token behavior.
Explicit floors below 16,000 tokens resolve to 16,000.
Initial and model-update threshold calculations use the same effective floor.
A deliberately reduced floor can permit an auxiliary model whose context window is below 64,000 but not below the effective floor.
Changing the floor invalidates and rebuilds cached gateway agents.

skills.title: Centralize configurable runtime policy and eliminate bypass paths
skills.summary: Resolve one effective runtime policy from configuration while preserving the legacy default, propagate that value through shared services and constructors, and replace direct platform-derived values, literals, and independently computed defaults across affected consumers. Enforce the policy at the narrowest shared boundary available so existing call sites inherit it consistently, while auditing readers, writers, and derived calculations for paths that bypass the canonical configuration source.
preconditions: A runtime behavior or resource location has a canonical configurable value and a compatibility default.
Multiple consumers can otherwise derive, embed, or retain inconsistent values independently.
The effective policy can be propagated to shared services, construction paths, or common enforcement boundaries.
failure_modes: Adding configuration without propagating it leaves consumers operating with an implicit or stale default.
Converting only prominent call sites leaves bypasses that violate the configured policy.
Changing the compatibility fallback while centralizing policy can regress existing installations.
Enforcing the policy too far from the shared boundary allows independent consumers to diverge.
